concepts.name: Tenant isolation: shared table, schema or database per tenant
Passing the tenant to Postgres per transaction
Filtering retrieval by tenant and permissions
Testing that one tenant can't see another's documents

questions.prompt: Your RAG product has 5,000 small tenants, each with a few hundred documents. Which isolation model fits best?

choices.text: A separate database for each tenant, for the strongest isolation
A separate vector database cluster for each tenant, so no index is shared
Shared tables with a `tenant_id` column that every query filters on
One table per tenant, created on sign-up so each tenant's rows stay apart

questions.explanation: Microsoft's multitenant RAG guide says store-per-tenant brings management overhead and cost and shouldn't be used for a large number of small tenants; it can also hit service limits. A shared (multitenant) store scales to many tenants cheaply. The price is that data isolation becomes your most important concern: every retrieval must carry the tenant filter.

sources.title: Design a Secure Multitenant RAG Inferencing Solution - Azure Architecture Center | Microsoft Learn
sources.claim: Store-per-tenant adds management overhead and cost, should not be used for a large number of small tenants and may hit service limits, while multitenant stores handle more tenants cheaply but make data isolation the most important concern.

questions.prompt: A large enterprise customer requires that its data never shares storage with other customers, and wants its costs reported separately. Which model fits?

choices.text: A database (store) per tenant
Shared tables with a `tenant_id` column
Shared tables with row-level security
A shared table with one column per tenant

questions.explanation: A store per tenant gives data and performance isolation: no noisy neighbours, and the whole store's cost belongs to one tenant. Shared tables, with or without row-level security, still keep that customer's rows next to everyone else's. Solutions often mix models: dedicated stores for a few large tenants, a shared store for the rest.

sources.title: Design a Secure Multitenant RAG Inferencing Solution - Azure Architecture Center | Microsoft Learn
sources.claim: A store per tenant gives data and performance isolation, avoids noisy neighbours and lets the whole store's cost be attributed to one tenant, and solutions can combine store-per-tenant with multitenant stores.

questions.prompt: Compare three ways to isolate tenants in Postgres: a `tenant_id` column in shared tables, a schema per tenant, and a database per tenant. When would you pick each?

model_answer.summary: The three trade isolation against cost and operational work. A shared table is cheapest and scales to many tenants but depends on every query filtering correctly; a database per tenant isolates best and costs the most to run.
key_points: Shared tables with `tenant_id`: cheapest and simplest to operate, fits many small tenants, but isolation depends on every query (or a row-level security policy) filtering by tenant
Schema per tenant: separates tenants' tables inside one database, but every migration must run on every schema, which gets heavy as tenants grow
Database per tenant: strongest data and performance isolation and clear cost per tenant, but the most instances to provision, migrate and monitor
The number of tenants and the data per tenant drive the choice, and mixing models (dedicated for large tenants, shared for the rest) is common

questions.explanation: Start from how many tenants you expect and what they require. Many small tenants push you to shared tables; a few large, regulated tenants can justify their own database.

sources.title: Design a Secure Multitenant RAG Inferencing Solution - Azure Architecture Center | Microsoft Learn
sources.claim: Store-per-tenant trades isolation and clear cost allocation for higher management overhead, multitenant stores are cheaper and scale to more tenants but need careful isolation, and the number of tenants and data per tenant drive the choice.

questions.prompt: You run `ALTER TABLE documents ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;` but create no policies yet. What does the application role (not the table owner) see when it runs `SELECT * FROM documents`?

choices.text: Every row, because row-level security does nothing until a policy exists
No rows, because with no policy Postgres applies a default-deny policy
An error saying the table has no policy
Only rows the role inserted itself

questions.explanation: With row security enabled and no policy, Postgres uses a default-deny policy: no rows are visible or can be modified. That fails closed, which is what you want for tenant isolation. Table owners, superusers and roles with `BYPASSRLS` are the exceptions: they bypass row security.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 5.9. Row Security Policies
sources.claim: If row security is enabled on a table and no policy exists, a default-deny policy applies so no rows are visible or modifiable; superusers, BYPASSRLS roles and (normally) table owners bypass it.

questions.prompt: A policy `USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid)` is in place, but in your integration test tenant A still sees tenant B's rows. The app connects as the role that created the table. What's the most likely cause?

choices.text: Policies only apply to `INSERT` unless you also add a `FOR SELECT` clause
`USING` is ignored unless the policy also has a `WITH CHECK` clause
The table owner bypasses row security unless you add `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`
Row security doesn't apply to tables with a `vector` column, such as embeddings

questions.explanation: Table owners normally bypass row security, and superusers and `BYPASSRLS` roles always do. Either connect the app as a separate, non-owner role, or use `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` so the owner is subject to policies too. A policy with no `FOR` clause applies to all commands, and `USING` works on its own.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 5.9. Row Security Policies
sources.claim: Table owners normally bypass row security unless ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, superusers and BYPASSRLS roles always bypass it, and a policy without FOR applies to all commands.

questions.prompt: A policy with no `FOR` clause has only `USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid)`. Tenant A's session tries to `INSERT` a row with tenant B's `tenant_id`. What happens?

choices.text: The insert succeeds, because `USING` only filters which rows are read
The insert succeeds, but the policy then hides the row from tenant A's reads
The row is silently rewritten to carry tenant A's `tenant_id` instead
It's rejected: with no `WITH CHECK`, `USING` is used as the check

questions.explanation: `USING` decides which existing rows a command can see; `WITH CHECK` decides which new or updated rows are allowed. Postgres documents that a policy like this implicitly gets a `WITH CHECK` identical to its `USING`, so the check applies to rows being written too. Tenant A can't write rows into tenant B's space.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 5.9. Row Security Policies
sources.claim: For an ALL policy with only a USING clause, the USING expression is also applied as the check on new rows, so inserts that fail it are rejected.

questions.prompt: Your app uses a connection pool. For each request it runs `SET app.tenant_id = '<tenant>'` and then queries tables protected by a policy on `current_setting('app.tenant_id')`. Why is `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction safer?

choices.text: `SET` is not allowed for custom settings like `app.tenant_id`, only `SET LOCAL` is
It's undone at commit or rollback, so the next request can't inherit the tenant
`SET LOCAL` pins the setting to the pool, so every connection sees the same tenant
`SET LOCAL` is faster because it isn't logged, so it can't leak into server logs

questions.explanation: A plain `SET` lasts for the whole session, and a pooled connection's session outlives the request. If the next request forgets to set the tenant, it runs as the previous tenant. `SET LOCAL` (or `set_config(name, value, true)`) is undone at `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. Outside a transaction block, `SET LOCAL` only emits a warning and has no effect, so run it inside the request's transaction.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: SET
sources.claim: SET without LOCAL lasts for the rest of the session once committed, SET LOCAL lasts only until the end of the current transaction, and SET LOCAL outside a transaction block emits a warning and has no effect.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 9.28. System Administration Functions
sources.claim: set_config(name, value, true) applies the value only for the current transaction.

questions.prompt: On a fresh connection that has never set `app.tenant_id`, a query hits the policy `USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid)`. What happens?

choices.text: The query returns every row, because a missing setting counts as a match
The query returns rows with a `NULL` `tenant_id`
The query fails, because `current_setting` throws an error for a setting that doesn't exist
Postgres uses the tenant from the previous session

questions.explanation: `current_setting(name)` raises an error when the setting doesn't exist, unless you pass `missing_ok = true`, in which case it returns `NULL`. Either way the query fails closed: an error, or a `NULL` comparison that matches no rows. Custom settings like `app.tenant_id` are allowed because Postgres accepts any two-part name as a placeholder.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 9.28. System Administration Functions
sources.claim: current_setting(setting_name) throws an error if there is no such setting unless missing_ok is true, in which case it returns NULL.

questions.prompt: Why must the tenant filter be applied in the retrieval query, rather than by telling the model to ignore other tenants' documents? Where should the tenant ID come from?

model_answer.summary: Access control has to happen before any text reaches the model, because a prompt instruction is not a security boundary. The tenant comes from the authenticated identity on the server, never from anything the user or the model can change.
key_points: Filter by tenant (and by the user's permissions) in the retrieval query, before any chunk is added to the prompt
An instruction to the model can be ignored or overridden, for example by prompt injection, so once another tenant's text is in the context it can leak
The tenant ID comes from the authenticated session or token on the server, not from the request body, the query text or model output
Every retrieval path applies the filter, including tools an agent calls in its loop, ideally through one data-access layer

questions.explanation: Microsoft's multitenant RAG guidance says to apply security filtering to every retrieval request, whether the app retrieves before calling the model or an agent retrieves during its loop, and to put the data access behind one API layer that enforces it.

sources.title: Design a Secure Multitenant RAG Inferencing Solution - Azure Architecture Center | Microsoft Learn
sources.claim: Every retrieval request against a shared store must include the tenant discriminator and user authorization filters, applied before grounding data reaches the model and also when an agent retrieves during its loop, ideally behind a single API layer.

questions.prompt: With pgvector, `SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY embedding <=> $2 LIMIT 10` uses an HNSW index. A small tenant owns 1% of the rows and often gets fewer than 10 results. Why?

choices.text: Row-level security hides some of the tenant's own rows from its HNSW index scans
The `<=>` operator ignores `WHERE` clauses whenever an HNSW index is used for ordering
`LIMIT` is applied before `ORDER BY` when an index is used
The filter runs after the index scan, which returns about `hnsw.ef_search` (40) rows

questions.explanation: pgvector applies the `WHERE` filter after scanning the approximate index. With the default `hnsw.ef_search` of 40 and a filter matching 1% of rows, few candidates survive. Fixes: iterative index scans (`SET hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order` or `relaxed_order`, pgvector 0.8.0+), a partial index or partition per large tenant, or a B-tree index on `tenant_id` for exact search over a small tenant's rows.

sources.title: GitHub - pgvector/pgvector: Open-source vector similarity search for Postgres
sources.claim: With approximate indexes pgvector applies filtering after the index scan, and with the default hnsw.ef_search of 40 a selective filter returns few rows; iterative scans (hnsw.iterative_scan strict_order or relaxed_order, 0.8.0+), partial indexes, partitioning or a B-tree index on the filter column are the remedies.

questions.prompt: Describe an automated test that proves one tenant can't see another tenant's documents in your RAG.

model_answer.summary: Seed two tenants with documents that would both match the same query, retrieve through the app's own code as one tenant, and assert that nothing from the other tenant comes back.
key_points: Seed two tenants with near-identical documents, so a missing filter would surely return the other tenant's chunks
Call the same retrieval function the app uses, authenticated as tenant A, rather than writing a separate query in the test
Assert that every result belongs to tenant A and that tenant B's content never appears, and that A still gets its own results
Run as the app's real database role (not the owner or a superuser, which bypass row security), and also check that a missing tenant returns nothing or an error
Run it in CI so a later change can't quietly remove the filter

questions.explanation: A test that writes its own `WHERE tenant_id = ...` query tests the test, not the app. The value of this test comes from going through the real code path with data that would leak if the filter were missing.

questions.prompt: Which test actually shows that tenant A can't retrieve tenant B's documents?

choices.text: Seed only tenant A's documents and check that A's query returns them
Query the table directly in the test with `WHERE tenant_id = 'A'` and check that no B rows appear
Seed A and B with near-identical documents, call the app's retrieval code as A, and assert every result has A's `tenant_id`
Ask the model in an eval whether its answer mentioned tenant B

questions.explanation: Only option c exercises the real code path with data that would leak if the filter were missing. With no tenant B data there is nothing to leak; a hand-written query tests the test instead of the app; and asking the model checks its wording, not what was retrieved.

questions.prompt: Which tradeoffs apply to multitenant grounding-data storage? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Separate stores can improve data and performance isolation.
Shared stores can reduce the number of instances to manage.
Separate stores eliminate all provisioning and management overhead.
Shared stores automatically prevent cross-tenant access without filters.
Tenant count and data volume influence the isolation model.

questions.explanation: A: Microsoft lists these as store-per-tenant benefits. B: Multitenant stores can reduce management and cost. C: Dedicated stores increase management overhead and may hit service limits. D: Shared storage requires secure tenant and authorization filtering. E: The architecture guidance uses both to choose a model.

questions.prompt: Which boundaries secure retrieval in a shared multitenant RAG store? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Retrieve all tenants’ documents and ask the model to hide unauthorized text.
Apply tenant and user authorization filters before grounding reaches the model.
Propagate the authenticated identity through downstream requests.
Apply filtering to retrieval tools inside an agent execution loop.
Trust a tenant name generated by the model as the authoritative identity.

questions.explanation: A: Unauthorized data must not enter the model context in the first place. B: Microsoft explicitly requires filtering before passing grounding data. C: The authenticated identity lets downstream components enforce access. D: The same requirement applies to every retrieval path. E: Tenant context must be derived from authenticated identity rather than model claims.

questions.prompt: Which practices make PostgreSQL tenant-isolation tests meaningful? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Exercise the application’s data-access path as its ordinary database role.
Use a superuser so the test confirms normal row-security enforcement.
Remember that table owners normally bypass row security.
Assume a `BYPASSRLS` role is constrained by every tenant policy.
Validate the centralized retrieval API’s filtering behavior.

questions.explanation: A: The role and access path must represent production authorization. B: Superusers bypass RLS and do not test an ordinary role’s constraints. C: Owners normally bypass RLS unless forced to obey it. D: BYPASSRLS explicitly bypasses the security system. E: The recommended single API boundary is designed to simplify validation.
